transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Mendez (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Cascade - Head of Product), Arjun Patel (Cascade - ML Eng), Samir Rao (Cascade - CTO)
Link to deck: https://app.redwood/example-deck (shared)

Summary (auto): quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation: streaming, core params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/ idempotency patterns, and a small live demo. Customer interested in cost/latency tradeoffs and onboarding a POC.

00:00 Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm lena from redwood, and diego's gonna run through the demo today, quick agenda — hosted api basics, streaming, params, and best practices for retries & cost.
00:12 Maya Singh: thanks lena, super excited — we want to see how this will fit into our chat assistant flow, latency is important for us.
00:18 Diego Mendez: cool, i'll share my screen — give me one sec, should be up.
00:34 Diego Mendez: alright screen's up, first thing — the hosted api is rest/ sdk first, you send a chat messages payload, pick a model from the catalog, and you can stream tokens back in real time. example call here — note the streaming chunk format, and you get partial deltas as they arrive.
00:50 Maya Singh: is streaming server-sent events or websockets?
00:55 Diego Mendez: we support both; the web demo uses SSE by default, and our sdk wraps it. for high-throughput low-latency clients you can use websocket streams. small note: if you use streaming you should design idempotency keys for chunk replay during reconnects.
01:15 Arjun Patel: how do you handle retries? we have flaky mobile networks and need at-most-once or at-least-once guarantees.
01:23 Diego Mendez: great question — common pattern: use a client-generated idempotency key at the request level; for non-streaming you can safely retry if a request fails before a response is committed. with streaming, you get partials, so we recommend checkpointing the last message token index and either resuming with a resume token or starting a fresh call and deduping on your side. we'll share a sample retry wrapper.
01:46 Samir Rao: cost wise, streaming vs non-streaming — any cost difference?
01:51 Diego Mendez: tokens billed the same; streaming just sends tokens earlier. where cost comes in is max_tokens, temperature affects output length distribution, and you can set top_p or stop sequences to constrain length. also our optimize tooling can suggest quantized model variants for cheaper per-token cost for certain workloads.
02:10 Lena Park: just to add, you can also route requests based on policy — region, latency SLO, or cost tier — so non-critical traffic can go to lower-cost models.
02:22 Maya Singh: what's the default tokenization? are we billed on input + output?
02:26 Diego Mendez: yes billed input + output tokens. we expose token counts in responses and console, you can see breakdown per request in the console trace. tokenization follows the model tokenizer (we include examples in the docs).

03:00 Diego Mendez (demo): i'm going to run a small chat demo — prompt is our assistant persona plus product context. sending request now... (typing noises)
03:22 System: [partial stream] "Hi, I'm Cascade Assistant. How can I help today?"
03:28 Maya Singh: wow that's fast — what latency are we seeing?
03:31 Diego Mendez: you should see ~80-150ms first token for a small model in hosted regions, depends on model & sequence length. we have perf profiles per model in the catalog — i'll point those out in the deck.
03:45 Arjun Patel: can we pin model versions? we need deterministic outputs for evaluation.
03:49 Lena Park: yes, you can pin to a model version and use rollout policies — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant if capacity's constrained.
04:05 Maya Singh: security — for hosted, do you offer SSO, enterprise RBAC, and logs?
04:10 Lena Park: yes — SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC roles, audit logs, and optional log redaction. for data at rest we integrate with customer KMS for encryption-on-key. we'll share SOC2 and network diagram.

05:00 Diego Mendez: back to params — temperature: controls randomness; typical range 0-1, lower = deterministic. top_p: nucleus sampling; you can use either. max_tokens: cap the output length — good for cost control. stop sequences: ensure assistant stops on your markers.
05:28 Maya Singh: what about top_k or repetition penalty?
05:31 Diego Mendez: model dependent — some models support top_k and repetition penalties via the param set. our sdk surfaces supported params per model.

06:00 Arjun Patel: we run heavy multi-turn chat with long contexts — any KV cache or prefix caching to improve latency?
06:07 Diego Mendez: yes, we have prefix / KV cache that caches key/value kvs for recent contexts to avoid recomputing past layers. note some customers reported the transcript generator mislabels it as K V cache — but it's the same idea. cache invalidation policies are configurable.
06:25 Samir Rao: how do you measure quality regressions during model updates?
06:30 Lena Park: our optimize tool ties evals to prompt sets; you can run canary evals and get regression alerts if metrics drop. we keep versioned eval histories.

08:00 Diego Mendez (live code): here's a python snippet — client.chat.create(model="redwood-medium-v1", messages=[...], temperature=0.2, max_tokens=150, stream=True, idempotency_key="cascade-1234")
08:20 Diego Mendez: note the idempotency_key parameter. for retries wrap the call and if the client didn't commit response, you can retry with same key and we will dedupe. small caveat: streaming partials still need application-level logic.

10:10 Maya Singh: if we hit rate limits, do you provide backoff headers or a retry-after?
10:15 Diego Mendez: yes we return standard retry-after and x-rate-limit headers. we also expose per-route quotas in the console and allow you to request burst increases.

12:00 Arjun Patel: what about on-prem / private deployment? we have PHI in some contexts and may need a private instance.
12:06 Lena Park: we offer Redwood Private — control plane in your VPC or on-prem package for air-gapped installs. security team will handle SAs; for hosted POC most customers start with strict NDAs plus data retention options, then move to private if required.
12:25 Samir Rao: great. any other enterprise concerns like data residency?
12:28 Lena Park: yes region pinning and data residency options available; we'll include the compliance pack.

15:00 Diego Mendez: quick note on retry patterns we recommend: idempotency at request level, exponential backoff with jitter, and detect partial streams by checkpointing last token; if partial, either resume (if using resume tokens) or re-call and dedupe. we'll attach a sample library.

18:00 Maya Singh: are there SDKs for mobile?
18:03 Diego Mendez: yes — official js/python SDKs and community mobile wrappers, but we generally recommend calling from a server-side proxy for key safety and to manage quotas.

22:00 Diego Mendez (demo #2): small prompt showing stop sequences and streaming chunking. sending now...
22:30 System: [stream] "Sure — here's the plan:
1) Gather inputs
2) Draft reply
3) Confirm tone
[STREAM END]"
22:45 Maya Singh: for long form exports we need structured output (json) — can your function/tool calling do that?
22:51 Diego Mendez: yes we support structured output and function calling style responses; we can enforce strict schemas and validate on the runtime.

28:00 Lena Park: recap: customer wants to run a small POC to validate latency and cost vs current provider, include privacy/ security checklist.
28:10 Maya Singh: correct, we'll run 2 scenarios: short chat assistant and long-form summary generation — we'll send sample prompts.

33:00 Diego Mendez: next i'll share a benchmark script that runs 100 requests across sample models and reports p50/p95 latencies and token cost; it's lightweight and reproducible.

36:00 Samir Rao: timeline — we want results before year-end if possible. can you commit to resources?
36:08 Lena Park: yes we can prioritize a POC kickoff on 2026-12-22 and assign an engineer for onboarding.

40:00 Maya Singh: any gotchas for streaming into our mobile app?
40:10 Diego Mendez: watch for reconnect logic and idempotency; use short max_tokens on mobile; also consider server-side response compression and chunk coalescing.

43:00 Lena Park: ok i'll recap the action items and we'll follow up by end of day with the materials.
43:10 Maya Singh: perfect thanks everyone.
43:20 Diego Mendez: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
